quizzes.title: Key terms and ideas
quizzes.intro: Ten quick checks on the vocabulary of cost-volume-profit analysis.

questions.q: Which quantity is revenue minus all costs that vary with the number of output units?
questions.explain: Contribution margin is defined as revenues minus all variable costs; operating profit also deducts fixed cost, and gross margin deducts cost of goods sold.

questions.q: Unit contribution margin (UCM) is
options: Unit sales price + unit variable cost
Unit sales price − unit variable cost
Unit variable cost ÷ unit sales price
questions.explain: UCM = USP − UVC, the amount each unit sold leaves to cover fixed cost. Fixed cost ÷ units is fixed cost per unit, a different idea.

questions.q: The break-even point is the quantity at which
questions.explain: At break-even TR = TVC + TFC, so profit is zero. Contribution is not zero there — it exactly equals fixed cost.

questions.q: At the break-even point total contribution equals total fixed cost.
questions.explain: Break-even means revenue equals total cost, so contribution (revenue − variable cost) exactly covers the fixed cost and profit is zero.

questions.q: In the juice-stall example, which cost is the fixed cost?
options: The Rs 6 paid per unit of juice
questions.explain: The stall costs Rs 5,000 whether one glass or a thousand are sold, so it is fixed; the Rs 6 purchase cost varies with units sold.

questions.q: Sensitivity analysis in CVP asks
options: How the units needed change when fixed cost, variable cost or profit target change
Which customers are sensitive to price
How to measure the gross margin
questions.explain: The lecture's sensitivity table recomputes units to sell for different combinations of fixed cost, unit variable cost and target profit.

questions.q: The contribution margin ratio is
questions.explain: The ratio expresses contribution as a fraction of sales: Rs 4 ÷ Rs 10 = 40 % in the lecture calculator. Profit ÷ revenue is the profit margin.

questions.q: Gross margin and contribution margin are two names for the same figure.
questions.explain: Contribution margin deducts only variable costs; gross margin deducts cost of goods sold, which includes fixed manufacturing cost. The lecture lists them as separate ideas.

questions.q: To find the units needed for a target profit, you
options: Subtract the target profit from fixed cost before dividing by UCM
Add the target profit to fixed cost and divide by UCM
Divide the target profit by the selling price
Multiply break-even units by the target profit
questions.explain: Q = (TFC + target profit) ÷ UCM. The profit is treated like an extra fixed amount that contribution must cover.

questions.q: Why did it matter that unsold juice could be returned in the lecture example?
options: It made the selling price higher
It kept the juice cost strictly variable — only units sold cost Rs 6
It changed the contribution margin ratio
questions.explain: If unsold units could not be returned, the juice bought would become a cost regardless of sales; returnability makes the Rs 6 vary exactly with units sold.

quizzes.title: Formulas and relationships
quizzes.intro: The break-even equation and how the answer moves when each input moves.

questions.q: Starting from USP × Q = UVC × Q + TFC, the break-even quantity is
questions.explain: Collecting Q gives Q × (USP − UVC) = TFC, so Q = TFC ÷ UCM. Dividing by USP alone ignores the variable cost.

questions.q: If the fixed cost rises and nothing else changes, the break-even quantity
questions.explain: Q = TFC ÷ UCM, so a larger numerator means more units are needed; in the sensitivity table each step in fixed cost raises every row of units.

questions.q: If the unit variable cost rises while the selling price is unchanged, the unit contribution margin
questions.explain: UCM = USP − UVC, so a higher UVC shrinks the contribution and therefore raises the break-even point.

questions.q: Doubling the fixed cost doubles the break-even quantity when the unit contribution margin is unchanged.
questions.explain: Break-even quantity is proportional to fixed cost: Q = TFC ÷ UCM. With UCM constant, twice the fixed cost needs twice the units.

questions.q: Revenue at the break-even volume equals
options: Total fixed cost + total variable cost at that volume
questions.explain: By definition revenue equals total cost at break-even: Rs 12,500 = 5,000 fixed + 6 × 1,250 variable in the lecture example.

questions.q: The profit at any volume Q above break-even equals
questions.explain: Each unit beyond break-even adds one full unit contribution, since fixed cost is already covered. Q × UCM is total contribution, not profit.

questions.q: Break-even revenue in rupees can be found as
questions.explain: Rs 5,000 ÷ 0.40 = Rs 12,500, which matches 1,250 units × Rs 10. Multiplying by the ratio instead gives Rs 2,000, far too small.

questions.q: In the sensitivity table, moving across a row from 'Profit 0' to 'Profit 2,000' at a fixed cost of Rs 4,000 and UCM Rs 4, the units rise from 1,000 to
questions.explain: (4,000 + 2,000) ÷ 4 = 1,500 units. 1,250 is the figure for a profit of Rs 1,000; 2,000 would need a UCM of Rs 3.

questions.q: If the selling price is raised and the variable cost is unchanged, fewer units are needed to break even.
questions.explain: A higher price increases UCM, the denominator of TFC ÷ UCM, so the break-even quantity falls.

questions.q: Which combination gives the LOWEST break-even quantity?
questions.explain: Q = TFC ÷ UCM is smallest when the numerator is small and the denominator is large; in the table that is the Rs 4,000 / UCM Rs 5 row at 800 units.

quizzes.title: Worked calculations
quizzes.intro: Break-even and target-profit arithmetic with the juice-stall numbers and a few textile variations.

questions.q: Juice is bought at Rs 6 and sold at Rs 10; the stall costs Rs 5,000. How many glasses must be sold to break even?
questions.explain: UCM = 10 − 6 = Rs 4; break-even = 5,000 ÷ 4 = 1,250 glasses.

questions.q: With USP Rs 10, UVC Rs 6 and fixed cost Rs 5,000, how many units must be sold to earn a profit of Rs 2,000?
questions.explain: Units = (5,000 + 2,000) ÷ 4 = 1,750, matching the sensitivity table row for fixed cost 5,000 and UCM 4.

questions.q: Selling price Rs 10, unit variable cost Rs 7, fixed cost Rs 6,000. How many units are needed to break even?
questions.explain: UCM = 10 − 7 = Rs 3; 6,000 ÷ 3 = 2,000 units — the last row of the sensitivity table.

questions.q: Selling price Rs 10, unit variable cost Rs 5, fixed cost Rs 4,000, target profit Rs 1,500. Units to sell?
What is the revenue at the break-even volume when 1,250 units are sold at Rs 10 each?
questions.explain: Revenue = 1,250 × 10 = Rs 12,500, which equals total cost 5,000 + 6 × 1,250 = 12,500.

questions.q: Selling price Rs 10 and unit variable cost Rs 6. What is the contribution margin ratio as a percentage?
questions.explain: Ratio = UCM ÷ USP = 4 ÷ 10 = 40 %.

questions.q: If 1,600 glasses are sold at Rs 10 with juice cost Rs 6 and stall cost Rs 5,000, what is the profit?
A towel unit sells at Rs 450 per piece with variable cost Rs 330 per piece and monthly fixed cost Rs 1,800,000. Break-even pieces per month?
Fixed cost Rs 5,000, USP Rs 10, UVC Rs 7, target profit Rs 1,000. Units to sell (to the nearest unit) are
questions.explain: (5,000 + 1,000) ÷ 3 = 2,000 units. 1,667 is break-even alone; 1,500 uses UCM Rs 4 by mistake.

questions.q: A product has contribution margin ratio 25 % and fixed cost Rs 200,000. Break-even revenue is
questions.explain: Break-even revenue = 200,000 ÷ 0.25 = Rs 800,000. Rs 50,000 comes from multiplying by the ratio instead of dividing.

quizzes.title: Applied in practice
quizzes.intro: Decisions a mill or costing office faces where break-even thinking gives the answer.

questions.q: A mill can cut unit variable cost by Rs 1 by changing supplier, or cut fixed cost by Rs 1,000 a month. At USP Rs 10, UVC Rs 6 and fixed cost Rs 5,000, which lowers break-even more?
options: Cutting variable cost — break-even falls to 1,000
Cutting fixed cost — break-even falls to 800
Both give the same break-even of 1,000 units
questions.explain: UVC Rs 5 gives 5,000 ÷ 5 = 1,000 units; fixed cost Rs 4,000 gives 4,000 ÷ 4 = 1,000 units — equal here. Above break-even, though, the variable-cost saving adds Rs 1 of profit per unit, so it grows faster.

questions.q: Demand for a product is at most 1,200 units a month. With fixed cost Rs 5,000, USP Rs 10 and UVC Rs 6, the product
questions.explain: Break-even is 1,250 units, above the maximum demand of 1,200, so the product loses money at any achievable volume: a loss of 50 × 4 = Rs 200 at best.

questions.q: A costing officer is asked for the minimum price at which an extra 500 units can be accepted without loss, given fixed cost already covered and UVC Rs 6. The floor price is
questions.explain: Once fixed cost is covered, any price above the unit variable cost adds positive contribution; Rs 6 is the floor, and below it each unit loses money.

questions.q: If a mill is operating well above its break-even point, a small increase in unit variable cost will have no effect on profit.
questions.explain: Every unit sold loses that increase in contribution, so profit falls by the increase × units sold; being above break-even only means the mill stays profitable, not that profit is unchanged.

questions.q: A dyeing manager proposes renting a second stenter, adding Rs 2,000 to monthly fixed cost, to raise capacity. With UCM Rs 4, how many extra units must be sold each month just to pay for it?
questions.explain: Extra units = 2,000 ÷ 4 = 500. Multiplying by UCM (8,000) is the common reversal error.

questions.q: The marketing team wants a Rs 1,500 profit from the juice stall and can sell 1,500 glasses. At USP Rs 10, UVC Rs 6 and fixed cost Rs 5,000, they should
options: Accept — 1,500 glasses give exactly Rs 1,000 profit, which meets the target
Accept — the target needs only 1,250 glasses
Refuse — the stall cannot break even
questions.explain: (5,000 + 1,500) ÷ 4 = 1,625 glasses; 1,500 glasses give only (1,500 − 1,250) × 4 = Rs 1,000 profit, short of the target.

questions.q: A knitting unit has fixed cost Rs 600,000 a month, sells at Rs 180 per kg and has variable cost Rs 150 per kg. What monthly profit does it make at 25,000 kg?
Two plans: A has fixed cost Rs 4,000 and UVC Rs 7; B has fixed cost Rs 6,000 and UVC Rs 5, both at USP Rs 10. At 1,400 units, which earns more?
questions.explain: A: 1,400 × 3 − 4,000 = Rs 200; B: 1,400 × 5 − 6,000 = Rs 1,000. B earns Rs 800 more because the higher contribution outweighs the extra fixed cost at this volume.

questions.q: A supplier offers a discount that lowers UVC from Rs 6 to Rs 5 but requires a Rs 1,000 annual membership. At what annual volume does the offer start to pay?
questions.explain: Saving per unit Rs 1 must cover the Rs 1,000 fee: 1,000 ÷ 1 = 1,000 units. Above that the discount pays; below it the fee costs more than it saves.

questions.q: A costing office reports 'break-even 1,250 units' for a yarn with USP Rs 10 and UVC Rs 6, but the new year's fixed cost is Rs 6,000. The report should be corrected to
questions.explain: 6,000 ÷ 4 = 1,500 units; break-even must be recalculated whenever fixed cost changes.

quizzes.title: Challenge review
quizzes.intro: Harder questions across the lecture: reversed formulas, two-step reasoning and reading the sensitivity table.

questions.q: At USP Rs 10, a product needs 1,333 units to break even with fixed cost Rs 4,000 (rounded to the nearest unit). What is its unit variable cost?
questions.explain: UCM = 4,000 ÷ 1,333 ≈ Rs 3, so UVC = 10 − 3 = Rs 7 — the lecture table's third row.

questions.q: A student computes break-even as Rs 5,000 ÷ Rs 10 = 500 units. The error is
options: Dividing by the selling price instead of the unit contribution margin
Forgetting to add the target profit
questions.explain: Each unit contributes only Rs 4 (price minus variable cost), not the whole Rs 10, so the correct answer is 5,000 ÷ 4 = 1,250 units.

questions.q: Fixed cost Rs 5,000, USP Rs 10, UVC Rs 6. The mill actually sold 1,100 units. What was the loss (give a positive number)?
questions.explain: Contribution = 1,100 × 4 = 4,400, which falls short of the fixed cost by 5,000 − 4,400 = Rs 600 — equivalently (1,250 − 1,100) × 4.

questions.q: In the sensitivity table every row shows the same increase in units (250 at UCM Rs 4) for each extra Rs 1,000 of target profit, regardless of fixed cost.
questions.explain: Extra units = extra profit ÷ UCM = 1,000 ÷ 4 = 250, and fixed cost does not enter this step; in the UCM Rs 4 rows the units go 1,000 → 1,250 (profit 0 to 1,000) and 1,250 → 1,500 (profit 1,000 to 2,000) whether fixed cost is Rs 4,000 or Rs 5,000.

questions.q: A yarn sells at Rs 510 per 10 lb. Variable cost is Rs 35 per lb and monthly fixed cost Rs 11,400,000. Break-even in lb per month is
questions.explain: Price per lb = Rs 51; UCM = 51 − 35 = Rs 16; 11,400,000 ÷ 16 = 712,500 lb. Dividing by the price (223,529) or the variable cost (325,714) are the usual slips.

questions.q: Contribution margin ratio is 30 % and fixed cost Rs 90,000. What revenue is needed for a profit of Rs 15,000?
questions.explain: Revenue = (fixed cost + target profit) ÷ CM ratio = 105,000 ÷ 0.30 = Rs 350,000.

questions.q: Which change leaves the break-even quantity unchanged?
options: Raising USP and UVC by the same rupee amount
questions.explain: Break-even depends on TFC and UCM = USP − UVC; raising both price and variable cost by the same amount leaves UCM, and therefore the break-even quantity, unchanged.

questions.q: Two stalls: Stall 1 has fixed cost Rs 4,000 and UVC Rs 7; Stall 2 has fixed cost Rs 6,000 and UVC Rs 5; both sell at Rs 10. At what volume do the two earn the same profit?
questions.explain: Profit 1 = 3Q − 4,000; Profit 2 = 5Q − 6,000. Setting them equal: 2Q = 2,000, Q = 1,000 units. Above this Stall 2 earns more.

questions.q: If a mill's UCM is Rs 16 per lb and its daily fixed cost is Rs 380,000, then selling 1,000 lb more per day than break-even raises daily profit by
questions.explain: Beyond break-even each lb adds its full contribution: 1,000 × 16 = Rs 16,000. The selling price (Rs 51,000) overstates it because the variable cost must still be paid.

questions.q: Fixed cost Rs 5,000 and UCM Rs 4 give break-even 1,250. If the unit variable cost falls by Rs 1 AND the fixed cost rises by Rs 1,250, the new break-even is
questions.explain: New UCM = Rs 5 and new fixed cost = Rs 6,250: 6,250 ÷ 5 = 1,250 — the two changes cancel exactly. 1,000 ignores the fixed-cost rise; 1,563 ignores the UCM change.
